notes: \cpara{Opens with a paraphrase of Steven Kaas, who wrote as the Black Belt Bayesian: behind a dramatic failure lies a larger, quieter one that made it possible. The linked page could not be reached here, so the paraphrase is unchecked.}
\cpara{States the thesis: removing religion would leave in place the ``larger failures of sanity'' that made it possible. What those failures are is left to the lists further down.}
\cpara{Grants that religion is ``a direct problem'' worth fighting, and introduces the post's image for its other role: a dead canary in a coal mine, a symptom of larger problems.}

\cpara{The thought experiment: a course that never mentions religion, judged by how many students have lost their religion five years later compared with a control group. The design is testable. It is the kind of long, controlled follow-up the author asks for the next day in ``A Sense That More Is Possible'' (``survey them five years later'').}

\clogic{The question assumes that teaching general methods, without mentioning religion, would lower religious belief. The post gives no evidence for this. One later study of a nearby question gives it little support: among 806 college students, critical thinking classes that ``specifically and directly addressed pseudoscience'' reduced such beliefs, ``but research methods classes and unrelated general education classes did not'' (Dyer and Hall, \textsc{Research in Higher Education}, 2019). The beliefs the abstract names are in pseudoscience, extraordinary life forms and conspiracy theories, not religion.}

\cpara{Lists ten groups of the author's own posts as material for such a course. The post grants that they did not avoid religion, and says that one of them, Dark Side Epistemology, would be hard to teach without it.}
\cpara{Turns to a second argument: a scientist who is religious, or who casually endorses ``spirituality''. The link goes to ``Outside the Laboratory'' (2007).}

\cpara{The diagnosis of ``Outside the Laboratory'' again, now stated as knowledge (``We now know''). That post offered it as its own view (``to me'') and with ``probably''; our notes there say it rests on an imagined case, with no evidence about how real religious scientists reason. Here too, from the fact of belief alone, the post concludes that the whole list below is not being applied.}
\cpara{Calls these basic matters, and estimates, with a question mark, that an introduction to all of them would fill one four-credit undergraduate course.}

\cpara{Names two laureates. The link on Smalley goes to a comment that quotes his endorsement of a creationist book (``Evolution has just been dealt its death blow'') and two dated statements of his faith. For Aumann, whose own account of his religion differs from the post's picture, see the notes on ``Crisis of Faith'' and ``Changing the Definition of Science''.}

\cpara{Argues that the laureates are not isolated cases: colleagues who had taken the course would have corrected them, or pitied them too much to give them a prize. On belief itself, later figures support ``can't be isolated exceptions'': see the Pew survey of American scientists in the notes on ``Outside the Laboratory''.}

\cfact{This branch does not fit Smalley. He won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1996. The two dated statements the linked comment quotes are from October 2004 and May 2005, eight and nine years later; he died in October 2005. Wikipedia (``Richard Smalley'') says he ``rediscovered his religious foundation in later life''.}
\cpara{The conclusion: the waterline is ``really ridiculously low'', ``Even in the highest halls of science.'' For the highest halls, the evidence given is the two laureates above.}
\cpara{Restates the thesis in the post's image: throwing out the canary would make the mine stink less without raising the waterline much.}
\cpara{Ends by siding with the neo-atheists on the harm religion does, which it calls ``current and ongoing disaster''. That claim is asserted here, not argued.}
